readerTitle: Your rival opened first. Should you hurry?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 매장의 리필 스테이션, 항만 인근 냉장 창고) · 적용 레슨: 선발자 이점(STR-08-01), 빠른 추격자(STR-08-02)
insight: 먼저 출시할지 나중에 출시할지는 속도가 아니라 '먼저 가면 무엇이 잠기는가'로 정한다. 잠기는 것이 없으면 빠르게 따라가고, 있으면 먼저 차지한다.
misconception: 시장에는 먼저 들어간 쪽이 언제나 유리하다. 혹은 늘 기다렸다가 따라가는 쪽이 안전하다.

sources.text: Lieberman, M. B., & Montgomery, D. B. (1988). First-Mover Advantages. Strategic Management Journal, 9, 41–58.
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 두 사례(리필 스테이션, 냉장 창고)와 그 안의 숫자(매장 3곳, 상품 20종, 부지 2곳, 7년 계약, 공사 18개월)는 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
선발자 이점의 원천(희소 자원 선점, 전환 비용, 학습)은 Lieberman & Montgomery(1988)의 분류를 단순화한 것입니다. STR-08-01, STR-08-02 개념 레슨의 용어와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your rival opened first. Should you hurry?
body: A home-goods shop down the street puts up a new sign: *Refill station. Bring your own bottle.* Shoppers fill jars with dish soap and laundry liquid by weight.
You run three similar stores. Your first instinct is to rush. Your second is to wait. Both instincts can be right. It depends on one question.

image.label: A shop window with a new refill station sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 상점가. 한 가게 창문에 "Refill station" 안내판과 큰 세제 디스펜서들이 보이고, 맞은편 가게 주인이 팔짱을 끼고 바라보는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Do you add refill stations?
body: Refill suppliers are easy to find. Shoppers can walk to either store in five minutes. Nobody has to sign up or commit to anything.

options.text: Install stations in all three stores right away
options.feedback: You'd match the rival quickly, but you'd also pay to guess the product range and teach shoppers. **First-mover advantage** needs something to lock in, and here customers can switch in five minutes.

options.text: Watch the rival for a few months, line up a supplier, then launch a sharper version fast
options.feedback: This is the **fast follower** play. The rival pays to learn what sells, and you copy the lessons, not the mistakes. It only works if you're truly ready to move.

options.text: Wait a couple of years until refills are common
options.feedback: Low risk, but you give up years of sales and let the rival build habits with regulars. Following pays when it's fast, not when it's late.

cards.title: The first store does the expensive homework.
body: Here's how it often plays out. The rival stocks 20 refill products. Most sales come from three: dish soap, laundry liquid and hand soap.
Staff explain the system again and again. Shoppers forget their bottles, so the store starts selling jars at the counter.
Almost all of this is visible from the sidewalk. By watching, you get the answers without paying for the questions.

cards.title: Ask what going first locks in.
body: **First-mover advantage** is real only when an early lead turns into something rivals can't easily get later.
list: **Scarce assets:** the best sites, suppliers or permits
**Switching costs:** contracts or habits that keep customers from leaving
**Learning rivals can't see:** know-how that stays inside your business
cards.callout: No lock-in means going first mostly buys you costs.
cards.softwareNote: In software, lock-in often comes from data and integrations. A tool that customers wire into their other systems is costly to replace. A simple app anyone can copy in a month gains little by being first.

cards.title: Now it's cold storage near a port.
body: You run a logistics company. A port is adding a new terminal, and food importers will need refrigerated warehouses nearby. Only two sites near the terminal are zoned for warehouses.
A large importer wants a 7-year contract with whoever can open first. Building takes 18 months. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until the new terminal's volume is proven
options.feedback: You'd avoid demand risk, but both sites and the big contract could be gone. When the key assets are scarce, there's nothing left to follow into.

options.text: Secure a site and sign the importer before you build
options.feedback: This captures **first-mover advantage** where it truly exists: a scarce site and a long contract that keeps the customer. The signed contract also cuts your demand risk.

options.text: Rent refrigerated trailers for now and follow fast later
options.feedback: You'd learn cheaply, like a **fast follower**. But importers want long contracts, so the window closes the day the sites are taken.

cards.title: Same question, opposite answers.

breakdown.label: Nothing locks in
breakdown.detail: Shoppers switch in minutes, so follow fast

breakdown.label: Sites and contracts lock in
breakdown.detail: Scarce land and 7-year deals, so go first

cards.callout: The deciding factor wasn't speed or courage. It was what an early lead could hold on to.

cards.title: Following is a plan, not a pause.
body: A fast follower is busy while it waits: picking suppliers, training staff and preparing the launch. If you just sit and watch, you aren't following. You're late.

Lock-in can also change. If the rival in the refill story signed the only local supplier to an exclusive deal, waiting would suddenly cost far more. Check the question again whenever the market moves.

image.label: A runner crouched at the start line while another already runs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 트랙 위 두 사람. 한 명은 이미 달리고, 다른 한 명은 출발선에서 운동화 끈을 다 묶고 스타트 자세로 대기 중. '기다리지만 준비된 상태'를 표현. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Go first when it locks something in. Otherwise, follow fast.
body: You used two ideas from this unit. **First-mover advantage** told you when an early start pays: scarce assets, switching costs, hidden learning. **Fast followers** showed how to win second: let the pioneer learn, then move quickly.
**Try it today:** pick one idea you're considering. Write down what going first would let you hold that a rival couldn't get later. If the list is empty, plan to follow fast.
